before.exam_tip_html: For extended-response questions about international organisations, the most common error is treating them all as the same type of body. Examiners want you to distinguish between them: the UN is universal and focuses on peace and human rights; NATO is a military alliance; the Commonwealth is a voluntary cultural and development network; the Council of Europe enforces human rights via the ECHR; the WTO governs trade. For a 12-mark Evaluate question, pick ONE organisation, present the case for UK membership (security, influence, cooperation) AND the case against or for reform (cost, sovereignty, effectiveness), then reach a substantiated judgement — “On balance, UK membership of X is beneficial because… although critics raise valid concerns about…”. Also avoid the ECHR/EU confusion: stating that Brexit removed ECHR protections is a factual error and will cost marks.

For an 8-mark Discuss question on the PM’s powers, avoid simply listing powers — examiners want you to weigh them. Present one viewpoint (e.g. PM powers are necessary for effective government) and then a contrasting one (e.g. PM powers have grown too great, undermining cabinet government). Use a real-world anchor: name a specific event such as PMQs, a resignation over collective responsibility, or the 2010 coalition negotiations. For a 12-mark Evaluate, your conclusion must add genuine evaluative thinking: decide which argument you find more convincing and explain why, citing a named example. Phrases like “it depends” without further criteria do not access the top band.

For a 12-mark Evaluate question on political parties, you must present a genuine two-sided argument. A common error is to write only about one party’s beliefs or to list party policies without connecting them to underlying philosophical differences. Examiners reward answers that name the philosophical tradition (e.g. collectivism, liberalism, conservatism) and link it to a specific policy example (e.g. NHS creation as collective action, or low-tax policy as belief in market freedom). Your conclusion must make a substantiated judgement — for example, weighing which approach better delivers democratic choice for voters. Phrases like “both have good and bad points” without further reasoning will not access the top band.

The criminal/civil distinction is tested frequently in short-answer and extended-response questions. The most common errors are: (1) using the wrong terminology — calling the person who brings a civil case the “prosecutor” when the correct term is “claimant”; (2) stating that both criminal and civil cases use “beyond reasonable doubt” — civil cases use the lower “balance of probabilities” standard; (3) failing to link the standard of proof to its justification — examiners reward answers that explain why criminal cases use a higher standard (the consequences of a wrongful conviction include imprisonment). For 8-mark Analyse questions, you will usually be asked to analyse advantages and disadvantages of one system, or to compare the two. Always name a specific court (magistrates’ court, Crown Court, County Court, employment tribunal) or a specific outcome (damages, injunction, imprisonment) to demonstrate precise knowledge and reach the higher bands.

For an 8-mark Analyse or a 12-mark Evaluate question on voting systems, the most common error is to treat the answer as a list of pros and cons without making an explicit comparison or reaching a clear judgement. Examiners want you to weigh the arguments — for example: “FPTP produces stable majority governments, but at the cost of proportionality. The 2011 AV referendum showed that voters, at least at that time, preferred stability over greater proportionality. However, supporters of PR argue that fairness of representation matters more than ease of government formation.” Always name a real-world anchor: name a specific system (AMS, STV), name a specific election it is used for, or reference the 2011 referendum. A conclusion that merely says “both systems have advantages and disadvantages” without a judgement will not access the top band.

For an 8-mark Discuss question on devolution, avoid simply describing what devolution is — examiners want to see you weigh contrasting viewpoints. Present one view (e.g. devolution strengthens democracy by bringing decisions closer to communities) and then a contrasting one (e.g. devolution creates inconsistency and risks fragmenting the Union). Use a named example — reference the Scottish Parliament, the Senedd, or a specific policy difference between nations. For a 12-mark Evaluate, your conclusion must add genuine evaluative reasoning: decide which argument you find more convincing, supported by evidence. Watch out for the common error of confusing devolution with independence: state clearly that Westminster retains sovereignty, and that reserved powers (defence, foreign affairs, immigration) remain at Westminster level.

On an 8-mark “Discuss” or 12-mark “Evaluate” question about voter turnout or voting age, a very common mistake is writing a one-sided answer that only lists reasons for or against a proposal. Examiners reward responses that present both viewpoints, use connective language (“however”, “on the other hand”) and name a specific real-world example — for instance, Australia’s compulsory voting system, or the lower voting age in Scottish Parliament elections. For a 12-mark “Evaluate”, you must reach a substantiated conclusion: weigh which side has stronger evidence and explain why you reached that judgement. “It depends” with no further reasoning will not access the highest mark band. For the 4-mark “Source Interpretation” question, do not just summarise the source — identify what it shows, link it to your own knowledge and reach a judgement about what it means for democracy.

For an 8-mark “Discuss” or 12-mark “Evaluate” question on government spending, the most common mistake is writing a one-sided answer that either supports high public spending or criticises it without presenting the opposing view. Examiners reward answers that use connective language (“however”, “on the other hand”) and name a specific real-world example — for instance, the creation of the NHS, debates about welfare reform, or the distinction between health and social care funding. For a 4-mark “Describe” question, avoid drifting into evaluation; give two clearly described features and develop each one. For source-interpretation questions, do not simply list what the source says — reach a judgement about what it reveals and link it to your own knowledge of taxation or spending priorities.

For an 8-mark “Analyse” or 12-mark “Evaluate” question on how other countries are governed, a very common mistake is writing a vague comparison that does not name either country specifically or describe their actual features. Examiners reward answers that name the specific country, describe two or three concrete features of its system, and compare those features to the UK or to a contrasting system. Avoid value judgements that read as politically biased: write “critics argue that” or “supporters of this system contend that” rather than asserting one system is simply better. For the 12-mark Evaluate, you must reach a substantiated judgement — weigh the evidence and explain your conclusion. Simply listing facts about two countries without evaluation does not access the highest marks.

For an 8-mark “Discuss” question on how citizens bring about change, the most common error is simply listing methods without discussing how effective they are or presenting contrasting views. Examiners reward answers that use connective language (“however”, “on the other hand”), name a specific real-world example (the Hillsborough campaign, the Equality Act 2010, or the government e-petition system), and weigh the effectiveness of different approaches. For a 12-mark “Evaluate” question, you must reach a substantiated conclusion — for instance, arguing that the most effective method depends on the issue’s scale and the resources available to campaigners, and explaining your reasoning with evidence. For the 4-mark “Source Interpretation”, combine what the source says with your own knowledge and reach a judgement about what it shows — do not simply summarise the source.

On “Analyse” questions about pressure groups, the most common error is producing a one-sided answer that only lists advantages or only lists disadvantages. You must show two sides and weigh them. Always use a named real-world example — examiners reward the named anchor (e.g. the BMA as an insider group, the TUC as a union umbrella body, Citizens Advice as a civil society advocate). For “Describe” questions, stick to description; do not slide into evaluation. Two clearly described features — each with a brief developed point — is the target. Remember: pressure groups seek to influence policy, political parties seek to form a government — this distinction is tested frequently.

In the active citizenship section, a very common error is describing an action in vague, general terms without naming the specific issue, method and outcome. Examiners reward answers where you state: what the issue was (specifically); what action you took (what you actually did, not just “we campaigned”); what happened as a result; and your honest evaluation of whether it worked and why. For an 8-mark “Discuss” question, present contrasting views on the effectiveness of citizenship action using your own investigation as evidence alongside any wider knowledge. For the 12-mark “Evaluate”, your conclusion must add evaluative thinking about what makes citizenship action effective — not just a summary of what you did. Phrases like “we didn’t quite achieve our aim but we learned that ...” show genuine evaluation and can earn marks in the top band.
